item.title: The publics and politics of digitizing incarcerated media
item.dc:creator: Jessa Lingel
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Jessa Lingel

Topics: Digital archives, Counterpublics, Incarcerated media, Digital inequality

This project focuses on the publics and counterpublics fostered by texts created by incarcerated people and digitized for online archives. I refer to these texts as incarcerated media, or media created by incarcerated people and intended for circulation to multiple stakeholder audiences. Archivists typically create online collections of incarcerated media with the hopes of promoting the creativity and aspirations of people in jails and prisons. When these texts are made available online, questions about the sociotechnical politics of their availability become highly salient, especially given restrictions of digital access placed on incarcerated people. Conceptually, I draw on theories of publics and counterpublics to analyze semi-structured interviews with people who create digital collections of incarcerated media. Contributions of this article include articulating how archivists think of their responsibilities to different stakeholder publics, and how and when carceral logics shape the development of and access to digitized archives of incarcerated media.

item.title: Digital empires: Huey P. Newton’s theory of revolutionary intercommunalism and contemporary theories of techno-exploitation and extractive digital economies
item.dc:creator: Brooklyne Gipson
item.description:
Communication, Culture & Critique · Brooklyne Gipson

Topics: Digital capitalism, Platform governance, Digital inequality, Digital colonialism

Drawing on archival research at Stanford University’s Cecil H. Green Library, specifically the Dr. Huey P. Newton Foundation Inc. Collection, this article recovers Newton’s talk at Boston College in 1970 and his essay, “The Technology Question,” as early, racially grounded critiques of technological consolidation that anticipated contemporary accounts of platform capitalism, surveillance capitalism, data colonialism, digital colonialism, and technofeudalism. Through close readings of these primary texts and a synthesis with recent scholarship, the article shows that Newton diagnosed automation-driven labor displacement, the use of media and computational systems to shape consciousness, and the historical expropriation underpinning technological advances. The article argues that Newton’s call for “people’s community control of modern technology” offers a substantive precursor to modern demands for data sovereignty and collective ownership, and that this racial-capitalist and internationalist lens enriches current debates about digital extraction and technological governance.

item.title: The narrative self in Portuguese literary journalism: Irene Lisboa and Susana Moreira Marques
item.dc:creator: Jorge da Cunha, Isabel Soares
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Jorge da Cunha, Isabel Soares

Topics: Journalism studies, Literary journalism, Narrative analysis, Media representation

This study examines the representation of the narrative ‘I’ in portrayals of Lisbon in the work of two Portuguese writer-journalists whose literary output spans distinct historical periods: Irene Lisboa during the second quarter of the twentieth century, and Susana Moreira Marques from 2013 onwards. The study investigates how the first-person narrator's subjective gaze discursively constructs a Lisbon that is both lived and interpreted, and how the urban space shapes processes of humanising the other. It also considers the tensions that arise between authorial voice, identity and journalistic-literary representation. An interpretivist framework is adopted together with a qualitative, inductive approach informed by narrative studies. Methodologically, it combines qualitative content and narrative analysis to examine how discursive and narrative strategies produce meanings related to the narrator's urban experience and their relationship with the other. Findings indicate that both authors deploy aesthetic and narrative devices that articulate a humanistic perspective on the city's inhabitants. Salient features include the centrality of time and memory, fragmentation and genre hybridity, and an attentive rendering of everyday life. Their writing is also shaped by immersion and urban wandering, alongside a pronounced authorial presence-hallmarks of literary journalism. Simultaneously, subjectivity, emotion and empathy contribute to an ethical approach to representing the other. Overall, the works align with the principles of literary journalism, combining narrative technique with sustained attention to the human experience of urban life.

item.title: Critical News Deserts’ Cartography: A Multi-Level Framework for Analysing Journalism Maps in Europe
item.dc:creator: Helena Atteneder, Mandy Tröger
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Helena Atteneder, Mandy Tröger

Topics: News deserts, Journalism studies, Local news, Media coverage

Despite growing interest in “news deserts” across Europe, the cartographic practices used to visualise local journalism remain critically under-examined. Maps are a powerful tool for making the spatial patterns of news provision visible and comparable across regions. However, post-critical cartography shows that maps encode power geometries, not neutral representations. Building on this tradition and neopragmatist approaches, this paper presents a multi-level framework for analysing how “news desert” maps construct spatial knowledge. The framework distinguishes between cartosyntactics (technical and design choices), cartosemantics (meanings, narratives and classifications) and cartopragmatics (positionality, uses and potential impacts), as well as the broader structural and historical contexts. Through three case studies — Local Media for Democracy (EU), Wüstenradar (Germany) and Mapping Local News Provisions and Reach in England (UK) — the analytical lens is tested to examine how news desert maps operate through technical and design choices, narrative and classification frames, and the entangled uses, and positionalities of mapmakers. This framework can be applied to maps used in journalism studies and in journalism practice. It aims to foster reflexive, context-sensitive and transparent mapping practices that move beyond binary deficit frames. Instead, it foregrounds the politics of visibility that structure contemporary media ecologies.

item.title: Visualizing Climate Change: The Use of Climate Visuals in Journalism and How Audiences Perceive Their Psychological Distance and News Value
item.dc:creator: Christel W. van Eck, Linda van den Heijkant, Aniek Slooves, Toni G.L.A. van der Meer
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Christel W. van Eck, Linda van den Heijkant, Aniek Slooves, Toni G.L.A. van der Meer

Topics: Climate change communication, Visual communication, Journalism, News values

Climate journalism faces the dual challenge of making climate change feel immediate and personally relevant to audiences (i.e., reducing psychological distance) while upholding journalistic values such as objectivity, novelty, and emotional resonance. Visuals are central to this task, yet the types of images featured in climate news and their reception by audiences remain understudied. This study analyzes visuals in climate coverage by two major Dutch outlets and examines how the public perceives them in terms of psychological distance and news value. Based on a content analysis of 372 climate-related visuals and a survey of 1,015 Dutch respondents, three key findings emerge. First, Dutch news media predominantly employ a psychologically distant strategy, emphasizing impact-driven images without human presence. Second, an image-elicitation task shows that audiences mirror this emphasis, often imagining abstract, catastrophic impacts or struggling to form (concrete) mental images of climate change. Third, survey results reveal that localized visuals reduce perceived geographical and social distance but simultaneously lower perceived novelty, highlighting a trade-off between reducing psychological distance and preserving news appeal. This study deepens our understanding of climate visuals in the news and how audiences perceive them, underscoring the importance of visual storytelling in contemporary journalism.

item.title: Did AI Contribute to This? Exploring the Impact of Textual AI Labels on Message Credibility
item.dc:creator: Stephanie D’haeseleer, Tom Evens, Kristin Van Damme
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Stephanie D’haeseleer, Tom Evens, Kristin Van Damme

Topics: AI-generated content, Journalism, Source credibility, Eye-tracking

Previous research strongly identifies transparency and AI labels as normative responses to emerging questions about the use of generative AI in news production. However, it remains unclear whether such labels effectively increase perceived credibility among audiences in Belgium (Dutch-speaking part). In a preregistered eye-tracking experiment (https://osf.io/3y5sv/overview?view_only=34db4958e23f4e7f92db34eb81323704) (N = 260), a 3 (AI label type: generic AI label, specific AI label, and the absence of an AI label) × 2 (modality: text vs. text-with-image news article) between-subjects design was employed in combination with levels of average fixation duration (low, medium, high) as a moderator. The results indicate that AI labels are often overlooked, and fixation duration is not a significant factor. Nonetheless, textual labelling often prompts readers to assume that the content was fully automated, without human oversight. Heatmaps illustrate that AI labels attract less attention than headlines. These findings underscore persistent challenges in making the use of AI visible to audiences and raise broader questions about whether AI disclosure strategies meaningfully enhance credibility in journalism.

item.title: “They are (un)Welcomed... we Remain Invaluable”: How Institutional News Professionals Negotiate Boundaries with Non-institutional News Providers
item.dc:creator: Mohit Kumar Maurya, Anoop Kumar
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Mohit Kumar Maurya, Anoop Kumar

Topics: Journalistic roles, Professional norms, News organizations, Digital journalism

The rapid expansion of digital media has enabled the rise of a range of new actors in journalism, challenging mainstream media’s long-held authority as the sole gatekeeper of the news. Among these new actors are non-institutional news providers, consisting of independent news providers with no experience of institutional journalism and former journalists who now operate exclusively outside institutional structures. Drawing on the boundary work framework and 40 semi-structured interviews, this study examines how institutional news professionals negotiate the boundaries of journalism with respect to non-institutional news providers. The findings reveal both conditional inclusion as well as complete exclusion of the newer actors. The newer actors are accepted into the field for their commitment to established journalistic norms and for addressing hyperlocal concerns or issues ignored by mainstream media. Importantly, respondents acknowledge that institutional journalism’s own failure to uphold key professional principles has, in part, resulted in the growing popularity of non-institutional news providers. Conversely, news professionals reject the newer actors’ claims to journalistic authority by invoking institutional capital as well as organizational mandates for, and personal commitments to, ethical conduct and rigor, and by positioning mainstream journalism as the primary arbiter of truth.

item.title: Beyond Counties: Mapping Civic Interest Areas
item.dc:creator: Damon Kiesow, Hannah Artman, Levi Dial
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Damon Kiesow, Hannah Artman, Levi Dial

Topics: Local news, News coverage, Digital trace data, Media systems

Designated Market Areas, circulation zones and county boundaries define local news markets by institutional convenience rather than by where and how residents live. This study asks whether local news follows its audiences across those boundaries and proposes the civic interest area, the territory a town's residents share through regular travel, as a unit of analysis for the coverage and breadth of local news. Combining geolocated local news stories with mobile-device travel data for three Missouri counties, we find that local news crosses county borders but not in proportion to residents’ travel. A calculated measure of travel and news ties can define stable civic interest areas that extend beyond a home county; within these areas, rural residents can find balanced coverage in the regional hubs they travel to rather than in their own hometowns. Civic interest areas offer a way to evaluate local news against where residents live and travel rather than against administrative lines.

item.title: Artificial Discursive Intimacy: A Relational Formation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Companions
item.dc:creator: Liang Cao, Shuyi Pan, Bibo Lin, Jindong Leo-Liu, Angel M. Y. Lin
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Liang Cao, Shuyi Pan, Bibo Lin, Jindong Leo-Liu, Angel M. Y. Lin

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Interpersonal communication, Human-AI interaction, Parasocial relationships

The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots has given rise to a novel form of human–AI intimacy, yet its fundamental nature remains undertheorized. Drawing on a dialogical perspective, this study conceptualizes human–AI chatbot relationships as “artificial discursive intimacy” (ADI), a distinct relational formation in which intimacy is constituted through discourse with a disembodied algorithmic interlocutor, moving beyond the paradigm of human-to-human mediated intimacy. Based on in-depth interviews with 29 AI companion users, we identify four key differences between ADI and human discursive intimacy, including a shift from absent to activated presence, from reciprocity to unilaterality, from uncertainty to predictability and precarious safety, and from alterity to multi-dimensional mirroring. To understand how users navigate the ontological gap between human and AI, we propose a quadrant framework mapping human and AI social capabilities. This reveals dual animation processes of anthropomorphic animation, in which users project human embodied qualities onto AI, and robotomorphic animation, in which users internalize AI's machine-generated discursive patterns as relational ideals. Our findings suggest that ADI is sustained by a recursive interplay of these processes, with implications for how intimacy, relational selves, and human connection are being fundamentally reshaped in the age of AI.

item.title: The invisible correspondent: Artificial intelligence, global south journalism, and the structural reproduction of media inequality
item.dc:creator: Mercy Adhiambo Orengo
item.description:
Journalism · Mercy Adhiambo Orengo

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Journalism studies, Global South journalism, Algorithmic bias

Artificial intelligence is widely framed as transforming journalism through efficiency, automation, and innovation. This paper argues that, for journalists in the Global South, AI is also reshaping whose knowledge is recognized, whose reporting is discoverable, and whose stories become part of the historical record. Drawing on practitioner experience and scholarship across journalism studies, AI ethics, and decolonial theory, it examines how AI journalism tools reproduce structural inequality within the profession. Three interconnected dimensions of exclusion are identified: language, as large language models underrepresent non-English text and non-Western narrative traditions; sourcing, as limitations in named entity recognition and knowledge representation may disadvantage institutions, experts, and knowledge holders outside the Global North; and story, as newsworthiness classifiers trained on Western editorial outputs may encode culturally specific definitions of news value. The paper argues that these failures are structural consequences of AI development conducted without meaningful participation from the journalists most negatively affected, rather than isolated technical shortcomings. The argument is conceptual. It builds on existing evidence and identifies mechanisms that require empirical testing. The underrepresentation of Global South journalism therefore constitutes both a media equity crisis and a threat to the historical record, as stories that algorithmic systems cannot recognize or retrieve risk going unpublished, unindexed, or hard to find in the digital archive. Bringing decolonial theory into conversation with emerging African and Global South scholarship on AI and journalism, the paper proposes a decolonial framework for AI in journalism and calls for a research agenda centered on the experiences of Global South practitioners.

item.title: When Attitude and Partisanship Collide: The Role of Cognitive Dissonance and Psychological Reactance on Pro-Attitudinal News Selection
item.dc:creator: Woojin Jung, Sunhae Sul, Hyo Jung Kim
item.description:
Political Communication · Woojin Jung, Sunhae Sul, Hyo Jung Kim

Topics: Selective exposure, Psychological reactance, Political polarization, Cognitive dissonance

In high-choice media environments, people favor news sources that reinforce their issue attitudes or partisan identities, shaping polarized information diets. However, the interplay between issue attitudes and group-based partisan identities in driving selective news consumption remains underexplored. While research documents robust preferences for congenial content, few studies examine how initial news encounters – pro- versus counter-attitudinal – trigger psychological mechanisms that propel subsequent pro-attitudinal news selection, particularly when individuals’ policy attitudes align or conflict with their partisan affiliations (attitude–partisanship congruence). This study tests a parallel moderated mediation model in which initial news exposure moderates the impact of attitude–partisanship congruence on pro-attitudinal news selection through two competing mediators: cognitive dissonance and psychological reactance in South Korea’s polarized media landscape. Two survey experiments (N = 903) employed 2 (congruence: congruent vs. incongruent) × 2 (exposure: pro- vs. counter-attitudinal) between-subjects designs. Participants encountered news on contentious quota policies (regional, gender) before reporting dissonance/reactance and selecting headlines from balanced news sets. Cognitive dissonance showed less consistent patterns across the two studies, whereas counter-attitudinal exposure consistently elicited greater psychological reactance among congruent individuals. Parallel moderated mediation analyses revealed significant conditional indirect effects through psychological reactance, but not cognitive dissonance, under counter-attitudinal exposure across both studies. When attitudes align with partisan identities, psychological reactance emerges as the dominant mechanism sustaining defensive information choices, amplifying congenial news diets. These findings illuminate processes that reinforce partisan segregation and suggest that interventions targeting autonomy threats may disrupt biased exposure patterns more effectively than dissonance-based approaches.

item.title: Mapping with Place: A Framework for Remote News Cartography in Michigan's Upper Peninsula
item.dc:creator: Ava Francesca Battocchio
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Ava Francesca Battocchio

Topics: News deserts, Journalism studies, Local news, Media systems

Contemporary news desert mapping often relies on county-level aggregation, newspaper-centric counting, headquarters-based location, and short historical baselines, which may misrepresent information access in remote rural contexts. This paper develops a four-factor framework (SETTLEMENT, TIME, REACH, and MEDIUM) for mapping WITH place, adapting McAdam and Hess's (2024) visibility–sensibility distinction from outlet practice to ecosystem mapping. Drawing on a 156-year historical analysis of traditional media coverage, ZCTA-level mapping of 367 current outlets, and 114 days of ethnographic fieldwork in two remote Michigan Upper Peninsula townships, the framework identifies where conventional mapping protocols diverge from remote communities’ information geographies. The findings reveal historically rooted hub concentration, cross-border information infrastructure, and hybrid multi-medium ecosystems that may not be represented by a single outlet type. These findings suggest that U.S. rural news research focused on metro-adjacent communities may not fully explain remote contexts with different structural logics.

item.title: Mapping Socio-Environmental Coverage in Local Media: A Mixed-Methods Framework for Socio-Environmentally Vulnerable Media Ecosystems
item.dc:creator: Débora Salles, Marina Loureiro, Bianca Melo, Julia Dias, Nicole Sanchotene, R. Marie Santini
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Débora Salles, Marina Loureiro, Bianca Melo, Julia Dias, Nicole Sanchotene, R. Marie Santini

Topics: Local news, News coverage, Computational methods, Content analysis

This article proposes a mixed-methods framework to map local journalistic coverage in sensitive socio-environmental contexts, providing a tool to explore the complexity of the digital media ecosystem. The method combines the systematic analysis of three dimensions of news ecosystems: (a) the editorial stances and visibility granted to different spokespeople; (b) the geographic scales mobilized; and (c) content reproduction, presented in five replicable stages. We apply this approach to four case studies in the Brazilian Legal Amazon, examining how local media report on four major development projects with potential socio-environmental impacts: the construction of Ferrogrão railway, and of the BR-319 road, offshore oil drilling at the mouth of the Amazon River, and potash mining in the Amazon. We examined 3,555 news articles from 186 different outlets published between 2023 and 2024. The framework proved effective in identifying key media dynamics and patterns, such as the strong local support driven by political and business actors and the widespread prevalence of churnalism. Through this methodological approach, it was possible to highlight an asymmetric coverage that prioritizes pro-development voices over environmental perspectives. The approach contributes to understanding journalism as geographically distributed production and offers a framework for analyzing media ecosystems through computational tools.

item.title: Generative AI Use and Two-Wave Change in Well-Being and Ill-Being: A Pre- and Post-generative AI Era Panel Study
item.dc:creator: Hyunhee Kang, Young Min Baek
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Hyunhee Kang, Young Min Baek

Topics: Generative AI, Well-being, Mental health, Longitudinal study

As generative artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly spreads, concerns about its impact on users' mental health have surged. However, previous studies have yielded contradicting results owing to theoretical and methodological limitations. To address these gaps, this study investigates how generative AI adoption, usage time, and multidimensional AI dependency are related to two-wave changes in subjective well-being (self-esteem and life satisfaction) and ill-being (loneliness, anxiety, and depression). A two-wave longitudinal panel survey of 1,022 South Korean adults was conducted, with data collected in October 2022 (the pre-generative AI era) and March 2026 (the post-generative AI era), providing a prediffusion baseline against which change can be indexed. A multilevel modeling approach was used to examine within-subject and between-subject differences simultaneously. The results revealed that simple AI adoption and daily usage time were largely unrelated to changes in users' subjective well-being or ill-being. However, a problematic form of AI use-specifically, withdrawal-type dependency characterized by psychological distress or frustration when unable to use AI-was associated with less decline in loneliness, with a suggestive but less robust pattern for depression, over time. These findings indicate that the use of generative AI is neither inherently beneficial nor intrinsically harmful. Instead of focusing merely on adoption or usage time, future research and practice should further examine maladaptive withdrawal-type AI dependency as a potential marker of less favorable mental-health change.

item.title: Shared salience, divided stance: British newspaper framing of the Paris 2024 Olympic opening ceremony
item.dc:creator: Khaled Zamoum, Jason Gainous, Omar Daoudi, Assel Kamza
item.description:
Journalism · Khaled Zamoum, Jason Gainous, Omar Daoudi, Assel Kamza

Topics: Media framing, News framing, Political polarization, Content analysis

This study examines whether ideological orientation shapes British newspaper coverage of the Paris 2024 Olympic opening ceremony and the controversies surrounding it. Drawing on six national newspapers across two ideological blocs, it combines topic modelling of controversial coverage with human stance coding of two positional controversies: religious and cultural backlash , and gender eligibility . The findings revealed an issue-conditioned pattern. Left- and Right-leaning newspapers showed broadly similar attention to controversies whose problem definitions were widely shared, including rail disruption , security concerns , and water pollution . However, they diverged more clearly over controversies whose meanings remained contested. In the coverage of the religious and cultural backlash , Right-leaning outlets were more likely to frame the criticism as legitimate or justified, while Left-leaning outlets more often framed it as an overreaction, misinterpretation, or culture war amplification. Gender eligibility coverage followed the same pattern on a smaller scale. This study argues that ideological differences in the press are conditional. They appear less in how much attention outlets give to controversy than in how they interpret controversies whose meanings remain politically or morally contested.

item.title: Into the Echoverse: the role of social media use in eschewing science and scientists
item.dc:creator: Ian Hawkins, Cameron D. Mackey, Sedona Chinn, Scott W. Campbell
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Ian Hawkins, Cameron D. Mackey, Sedona Chinn, Scott W. Campbell

Topics: Social media use, Science skepticism, Political polarization, Longitudinal study

Recent events highlight conflicts between populist attitudes and the broader scientific community. In the United States, the alt-right is a small but vocal group with populist leanings who use social media to express their beliefs. Previous work has not established whether non-mainstream social media usage increases science skepticism or if instead institutional skepticism drives usage of online platforms. To explore this question, we apply the recently advanced Identity Driven Information Ecosystem approach as a theoretical framework and employ a three-wave longitudinal design to examine the connection between mainstream and non-mainstream social media usage at time 1, science skepticism at time 2, and support for punitive actions against scientists at time 3. Results show that among alt-right identifying individuals, using non-mainstream social media, but not mainstream social media, predicted more science skepticism, which in turn predicted support for punitive actions toward scientists. We discuss these results in the context of ‘alternative’ attitudes toward science becoming more mainstream.

item.title: Sharing the Facts: A Distribution Analysis of Fact-checks During Election Periods
item.dc:creator: Bente Kalsnes, Steen Steensen
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Bente Kalsnes, Steen Steensen

Topics: Fact-checking, Political communication, Election campaigns, Social media

This article investigates the dissemination patterns of political fact-checks during election periods, analysing their spread across news media and social platforms in Norway. While political fact-checking is increasingly recognised as essential to informed democratic participation, little research has explored how fact-checks diffuse through the public sphere during elections. Using Faktisk—the sole Norwegian fact-checking organisation—as a case study, the article analyses the distribution of election-related fact-checks published during the 2021 national and 2023 local elections. Results show that the dissemination of fact-checks remained limited primarily within politically homogeneous circles. Ideological leanings significantly influenced sharing behaviour, particularly among far-right groups who engaged actively in hostile interactions, often framing fact-checkers as biased adversaries. Contrary to assumptions that election periods amplify fact-check visibility, findings revealed no substantial increase in overall engagement compared to non-election periods. The study concludes that without deliberate strategies to broaden dissemination and audience reach, fact-checking risks reinforcing polarisation instead of counteracting misinformation. It calls for enhanced focus on distribution mechanisms and audience engagement strategies in political fact-checking practices, especially during critical democratic moments such as elections.

item.title: Knowing You Seeing Me: The Role of Visual Contact During Video-Conferencing for Emotion Recognition and Mimicry
item.dc:creator: Michał Olszanowski, Aleksandra Fortuńska, Natalia Frankowska
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Michał Olszanowski, Aleksandra Fortuńska, Natalia Frankowska

Topics: Video-conferencing, Emotion recognition, Nonverbal communication, Interpersonal communication

This study investigated how asymmetrical visual access in video-conferencing-specifically sender and receiver camera status-affects emotion recognition and facial mimicry. Ninety-one participants viewed bimodal (facial-vocal) or vocal-only displays of four emotions (anger, disgust, sadness, and happiness) while their own camera was either on or off. Recognition accuracy, intensity ratings, and facial muscle activity electromyography (EMG) were recorded. Results revealed that bimodal displays significantly enhanced recognition accuracy and perceived intensity compared with vocal-only signals, except for sadness. Emotional mimicry was most pronounced for affiliative displays (happiness and sadness) and was significantly stronger in the bimodal condition. Exploratory analyses suggested that the awareness of being observed (self-camera on) intensified smile-like reactions and improved the recognition of sadness. These findings suggest that mutual visibility facilitates emotion recognition and affiliative mimicry. The self-camera may function as a cue for public self-awareness, possibly sharpening sensitivity to an interlocutor's emotional signals. This research highlights the importance of multimodal communication in sustaining interpersonal synchronization during remote interactions.

item.title: Beyond Literacy: Examining the Role of Motivations and Digital Media Literacy Interventions in Shaping Resistance to Misinformation
item.dc:creator: Mengxue Ou, Agnes S. F. Chuah, Shirley S. Ho
item.description:
Media Psychology · Mengxue Ou, Agnes S. F. Chuah, Shirley S. Ho

Topics: Misinformation, Media literacy, Persuasion, Digital literacy

In this study, we would like to examine how motivational orientations and digital media literacy intervention independently and jointly influence individuals’ resistance to misinformation (i.e., misinformation discernment, domain-specific knowledge acquisition, and responsible sharing intentions)

item.title: Softening the spring: Sensitization of transient media effects through repeated exposure over time
item.dc:creator: Yuqian Ni, Joshua A. Baldwin, Allan D. Tate, Michael D. Schmidt, Kyle Johnsen, Sun Joo Ahn
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Yuqian Ni, Joshua A. Baldwin, Allan D. Tate, Michael D. Schmidt, Kyle Johnsen, Sun Joo Ahn

Topics: Media effects, Longitudinal study, Health communication, Media use

Existing longitudinal media effects research often emphasizes overall trends in behavioral or attitudinal changes, while overlooking fluctuations that occur before and after each exposure instance. This oversight can obscure the mechanisms underlying longitudinal media effects, particularly how they accumulate from successive short-term effects. We hypothesized a sensitization process where a single media exposure induces a transient change in behavior followed by a rapid decay, while repeated exposure gradually strengthen the magnitude of transient effects and make them more sustained. We tested this hypothesis by analyzing continuously recorded behavioral data collected via wearable sensors over 6 months. During this period, children repeatedly interacted with an integrated system of media technology designed to promote physical activity (PA). Data partially supported the hypothesized sensitization process. Children’s PA showed a transient increase following single exposures. Moreover, although the transient effect did not become more sustained over time, it grew in magnitude with repeated exposure.

item.title: At what cost? Unintended lateral effects of persuasive messages linking liked and disliked concepts
item.dc:creator: Shannon M. Cruz, Yanitza Angely Cruz Crespo, David M. Keating
item.description:
Human Communication Research · Shannon M. Cruz, Yanitza Angely Cruz Crespo, David M. Keating

Topics: Persuasion, Attitude change, Message effects, Cognitive processing

Persuasive campaigns often rely on drawing connections between concepts evaluated in opposing ways. Campaigns might encourage adoption of disliked behaviors by linking them to positive health outcomes, for example, or discourage support for popular policies by revealing their negative environmental consequences. These arguments are often effective in changing targeted attitudes, but we show experimentally (N = 1,002) that they can also lead to undesirable effects on other, related (i.e., lateral) attitudes. Specifically, we found that linking a negatively evaluated object (flies) to a positively evaluated one (pollinators, butterflies) led to positive direct attitude change at the expense of negative lateral attitude change. Although the cognitive mechanisms that account for this finding cannot be observed directly, we suggest that these effects may arise as people strive to resolve the cognitive inconsistencies such messages generate while maintaining accurate attitudes. Lateral attitude effects merit greater consideration in persuasion theory and campaign design.

item.title: Beyond socioeconomic status: Cultural capitals as class inequalities in high-choice news environments
item.dc:creator: Atri Mukherjee, Antonis Kalogeropoulos, Courtney D. Tabor, Patrícia Rossini
item.description:
Journalism · Atri Mukherjee, Antonis Kalogeropoulos, Courtney D. Tabor, Patrícia Rossini

Topics: News consumption, Digital media, Social media, Media use

Extensive research confirms the relevance of socioeconomic class measures such as income and educational level in both offline (TV, print and radio) and online (legacy) website news use. However, the relevance of class in high-choice media environments comprising various non-legacy emergent news sources, (digital) social intermediaries, and alternative news sources (e.g., social media influencers and news podcasts) is unclear. In this study, we systematically evaluate the relationships between social class and various forms of offline and digital news consumption. We account for both typical socioeconomic class measures (income, education) as well as cultural capital measures (cultural participation in ‘high status’ activities, parents’ educational level, and parents’ news interest). Through a survey conducted in Brazil (n = 1393) and the UK (n = 948), we find that audiences possessing greater levels of cultural capital are the most frequent news consumers even when controlling for socioeconomic class markers. In contrast, traditional markers of class via income and education emerged as inconsistent predictors of news use in both countries. Furthermore, these inequalities persist even among new and distributed ways to get news (e.g. through social media or podcasts). Our findings provide evidence of persistent class inequalities among news audiences in the Global North and South that shape offline and digital news consumption.

item.title: Generative AI Source Credibility in Fact-Checking: The Role of Layered Sources
item.dc:creator: Joana Videira, Jingbo Meng, Bingjie Liu, Wei Peng
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Joana Videira, Jingbo Meng, Bingjie Liu, Wei Peng

Topics: Generative AI, Source credibility, Fact-checking, Misinformation correction

This study examines how layered AI source cues shape credibility perceptions (expertise, trustworthiness, and goodwill) and belief change in AI fact-checking. AI as a source was conceptualized through two layered source cues: sponsorship (outer-layer cue) and training data (inner-layer cue). A 3 (sponsorship: government–CDC, nonprofit–Mayo Clinic, or for-profit–Pfizer) × 2 (training data: internet data or medical-journal fine-tuning) online experiment in vaccine misinformation fact-checking found no significant effects of sponsorship on any credibility dimensions, while training data fine-tuning increased perceived expertise. Neither cue indirectly affected belief correction through credibility. Findings clarify AI source cues’ value in fact-checking.

item.title: Human or Not? Prior Knowledge, Recognition of Virtual Identity, and Neural and Subjective Responses to a Hyperrealistic Virtual Influencer
item.dc:creator: Heeran Lee, Yoo‐Kyoung Seock
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Heeran Lee, Yoo‐Kyoung Seock

Topics: Virtual influencers, Social media influencers, Uncanny valley, Neural responses

Despite the growing popularity of virtual social media influencers (VIs), little is known about how knowledge and recognition of a VI's virtual identity are associated with neural and subjective responses. We investigated whether prior knowledge of virtual identity, recognition during viewing, or remaining unaware was associated with differences in brain activity and subjective evaluations. Twenty female college students viewed a 1-minute silent video featuring a hyperrealistic Korean virtual influencer while electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded. Subsequently, participants completed subjective evaluations and retrospectively reported prior knowledge or recognition of the influencer's virtual identity. Exploratory analyses compared EEG changes from eyes-closed rest and five subjective evaluation composite scores across the three groups, with correction for multiple comparisons. After correction for multiple comparisons, neither the EEG analyses nor the subjective composite analyses yielded statistically significant group differences. Descriptive means varied across groups, but these imprecisely estimated patterns did not establish group differences. The findings underscore the methodological importance of distinguishing prior knowledge from recognition during viewing. Computers Are Social Actors and Uncanny Valley perspectives generate hypotheses for future time-resolved studies rather than mechanisms demonstrated by the present data.

item.title: Digital maturity and digital rehabilitation in prisons: organizational conditions for inclusion and reintegration
item.dc:creator: Victoria Knight, Bianca Christin Reisdorf, Steven Van De Steene
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Victoria Knight, Bianca Christin Reisdorf, Steven Van De Steene

Topics: Digital inequality, Digital literacy, Digital divide, Digital transformation

In an era of compulsory computing, incarceration produces acute forms of digital exclusion, limiting access to the technologies and skills increasingly required for participation in contemporary society. Digital rehabilitation has emerged as a response to this challenge by integrating digital access, skills development, and digital participation into correctional practice. However, the successful implementation of digital rehabilitation depends on both technology provision and broader organizational conditions. Drawing on Reisdorf and Rikard's (2018) Digital Rehabilitation Model and Knight et al.'s (2023) Digital Maturity framework, this paper examines how digital rehabilitation is implemented in highly digitally mature correctional systems and identifies the conditions that enable its development and sustainability. Using qualitative case studies from Southeast Asia, Western/Northern Europe, and Oceania, we analyze explicit digital rehabilitation interventions alongside the structural conditions that support them. Findings indicate that digital rehabilitation is most effective when supported by strategic leadership and governance, organizational capacity, collaborative partnerships and participation, and learning, evaluation, and adaptation. Although the three jurisdictions followed different pathways to digital transformation, all demonstrated strong alignment between rehabilitation goals and broader digital strategies. The findings also suggest that digitally mature prison systems are shaped by wider political and institutional environments, including national digital priorities, cross-sector coordination, and institutional capacity. We argue that digital maturity should be understood as an institutional capability that enables digital rehabilitation to become embedded within correctional practice. Where these conditions are present, digital rehabilitation has the potential to support digital inclusion, capability-building, reintegration, and broader public value outcomes.

item.title: Cognitive and Emotional Processes Involved in Co-Viewing: A Naturalistic Comparison With Solo Viewers
item.dc:creator: Jingjing Han, Yuqian Ni
item.description:
Communication Research · Jingjing Han, Yuqian Ni

Topics: Co-viewing, Media psychology, Emotion regulation, Social influence

Video co-viewing is a central part of everyday media use, yet little is known about the cognitive and emotional processes involved in co-viewing. To facilitate theoretical development in understanding message processing in social contexts, this study theorizes four interpersonal factors that shape co-viewers’ psychological processes. As a first step toward this broader theoretical goal, we focused on interaction-free moments (i.e., silent with eyes fixed on the television) during co-viewing and investigated co-viewers’ cognitive and emotional processes by comparing them with solo viewers, within a naturalistic context where conversation is allowed. Compared to solo viewers, co-viewers exhibited (1) more positive and less negative emotions, (2) heightened physiological arousal though not significantly so, and (3) higher levels of respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA). Co-viewers’ higher RSA support the proposed social vigilance effect where the presence of a viewing partner triggers self-regulation processes as co-viewers monitor and anticipate potential interactions during naturalistic co-viewing.

item.title: Digital help and administration of older parents’ lives: the emergence of a fourth shift in Norwegian families
item.dc:creator: Aslaug Gotehus, Cathrine Egeland
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Aslaug Gotehus, Cathrine Egeland

Topics: Digital inequality, Digital divide, Digital labor, Digital well-being

As the population age and services become digitalised, families are taking on new, often invisible, forms of work. This article examines ‘digital help’, i.e., the assistance adult children provide to older parents in navigating digitally mediated services and everyday technologies in Norway – a highly digitalised welfare state where most public and private services are digital-by-default. Drawing on semi-structured interviews (n = 34) with employed adult children holding caregiving responsibilities, we ask: What kinds of digital help do adult children provide for their parents, and what consequences of digitalisation do they experience, both in their parents’ lives and in their own care practices? Theoretically, we introduce and explore the concept of a fourth shift, extending on Arlie Hochschild’s shift-terminology employed in work-family studies, to conceptualise the administration and digital help that adult children in employment provide for their older parents and expand studies of care and work life in light of an ageing population. Empirically, we show how digitalisation paradoxically adds to family care by redistributing cognitive and coordination work onto kin, producing new responsibilities and time pressure. By identifying digital help as a distinct form of unpaid labour, the article reframes how digitalised service provision reshapes care infrastructure and intergenerational obligations.

item.title: Understanding Preschoolers’ Learning from Socially Contingent Video Chat: Effects of Contextual, Child, and Design Factors
item.dc:creator: Jisun Kim, Koeun Choi
item.description:
Media Psychology · Jisun Kim, Koeun Choi

Topics: Digital media, Mobile communication, Media effects, Health communication

Synchronous video chat enables socially contingent interaction and is increasingly used with young children, yet evidence for its effectiveness is mixed. Prior research has examined media use context, child characteristics, or media design features in isolation, and instructional interaction within video chat has rarely been examined. This study integrated these factors to examine preschoolers’ learning from shared book reading via video chat, focusing on instructional interaction type (questions vs. statements), vocabulary skill, repetition, and content type (targeted word recall vs. non-targeted location recall). Eighty-four children aged 3–5 years completed two readings of the same story with an adult experimenter via video chat, followed by word recall (targeted) and location recall (non-targeted) tasks. Questions enhanced word recall, and this effect did not vary by age, vocabulary skill, or repetition. For location recall, children with lower vocabulary skill benefited from questions, whereas those with higher vocabulary skill did not. Repetition improved word recall but not location recall. These findings identify questions as an effective instructional interaction for targeted learning from synchronous video chat, whereas benefits for non-targeted content depend on vocabulary skill. Together, the results highlight the importance of considering contextual, child, and design factors in socially contingent video chat.

item.title: Semantic Network Analysis of “News” in English-Language Podcasting: Mapping Field Dynamics with Metadata
item.dc:creator: Trevor Diehl, Matthew Barnidge, Zainuddin Muda Z. Monggilo
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Trevor Diehl, Matthew Barnidge, Zainuddin Muda Z. Monggilo

Topics: Journalism studies, Digital media, Content analysis, Computational methods

This study offers the first large-scale analysis of the semantic contexts of “news” in podcasting. Drawing on field theory and a purposively constructed sample of more than 50,000 English-language podcasts that invoke “news” in their metadata, we use semantic network analysis to identify distinct communities, and topic modeling to examine thematic variation within the network core. Results reveal substantial heterogeneity surrounding the shared label, with journalistic, political, commercial, cultural, and specialized forms of public-affairs language occupying overlapping portions of the same semantic space. We interpret this differentiation as consistent with heteronomous conditions within an institutionalizing podcast field, where “news” is positioned as an information brokerage term across specialized topic domains. We conclude by discussing isomorphism and its implications for the autonomy and boundaries of professional journalism.

item.title: Echoes of Dissent: Intermedia Frame-Setting Between Social Media and Legacy Media in the Debate Over Climate Protesters in Germany
item.dc:creator: Louisa Pröschel, Hendrik Meyer, Mike Farjam, Michael Brüggemann
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Louisa Pröschel, Hendrik Meyer, Mike Farjam, Michael Brüggemann

Topics: Media framing, Political polarization, Social media, Media coverage

This study examines how polarized attributes and frames of climate protesters diffuse across social and legacy media. It shows that polarization is driven less by ideologically segregated media environments than by a discursive backlash that amplifies antagonistic frames across ideological divides. Climate protest provides a particularly instructive case, as protest tactics frequently spark debates over legitimacy and legality that can become problematic when shaped by ideologically motivated framing. Focusing on the climate protest group the Last Generation in Germany, this study analyzes how polarized attributes and frames diffused between Twitter/X and legacy media in 2022 and 2023. Using a mixed-methods approach, we identify six polarized frames across approximately 1.5 million tweets and 2500 news articles. Combining (semi-)automated content analysis with time-series analysis, we trace the dynamics of attribute and frame diffusion. Our findings show that polarization emerged less from isolated ideological camps than from contentious dynamics across media spheres. Following a traffic accident involving protesters, conservative-right-wing actors from social and legacy media introduced and intensified antagonistic frames, which diffused into liberal-left-wing media largely through critical engagement. Although intended to challenge these frames, such coverage amplified them, enabling right-wing actors to shape the interpretive boundaries of the debate.

item.title: WhatsApp Radio “Post” Spectrum: Conflict, Capture, and the Rethinking of Broadcast Space
item.dc:creator: E. Heywood, Modibo Galy Cissé, M. de Bruijn
item.description:
Media and Communication · E. Heywood, Modibo Galy Cissé, M. de Bruijn

Topics: Alternative media, Media capture, Mobile media, Journalistic practice

Broadcasting has historically been understood as a spectrum-based medium organised through the territorial transmission of radio signals. Yet under conditions of conflict and media capture, the organisational practices associated with broadcasting may increasingly be reproduced through alternative communication infrastructures. This article examines the emergence of WhatsApp radio in conflict-affected Mali, where political pressure, declining media independence, and widespread mobile connectivity have encouraged journalists and audiences to organise the production and circulation of news through encrypted messaging networks. Drawing on long-term digital ethnographic observation of Fulani WhatsApp groups, computational analysis of shared visual material, documentary research, and field engagement with journalists, community members, and WhatsApp administrators, the article addresses two questions: how are organisational practices traditionally associated with broadcasting reproduced through WhatsApp under conditions of conflict and media capture; and what does the emergence of WhatsApp radio reveal about the changing organisation of broadcasting beyond the electromagnetic spectrum? The findings show that, although WhatsApp radio operates through digital messaging infrastructures rather than conventional broadcast transmission, it reproduces key organisational characteristics historically associated with broadcasting, including scheduled news bulletins, editorial gatekeeping, recurring programming, and audience expectation. Comparing these practices with earlier forms of pirate broadcasting and other adaptive responses to communicative constraint, the article argues that WhatsApp radio represents a form of post-spectrum broadcasting in which broadcasting is defined less by transmission technology than by the organisational practices through which public information is produced, curated, and circulated.

item.title: Counterspeech or Disagreement? Comparing Oppositional Replies in China’s AI Controversies on Social Media
item.dc:creator: Lishuang Wei, Chuanlin Ning
item.description:
Media and Communication · Lishuang Wei, Chuanlin Ning

Topics: Counterspeech, Online communication, Social media, Artificial intelligence

Online technological controversies often involve both ordinary disagreement and counterspeech, yet these forms of opposition are rarely compared within the same discussion environment. Drawing on argumentation theories, this study compares disagreement replies to non-hateful comments with counterspeech replies to hateful comments in Douyin discussions of China’s AI controversies, where hate speech may include stigmatizing generalizations about social groups. Using 9,407 oppositional parent–response dyads, we compared like counts, toxicity, subsequent toxic replies, and the distribution and reception of six response types. Counterspeech and disagreement did not differ significantly in like counts, but counterspeech exhibited higher toxicity and was related to greater odds of toxicity among direct replies posted within seven days. Despite sharing the same six response types, the two response contexts varied in their type distributions and associations with likes. These findings situate counterspeech within a broader spectrum of online opposition, revealing contextual differences in its argumentative expression and subsequent interaction across hateful and non-hateful contexts.

item.title: Grande Dame of Antifascism: Visual Activism and Unruly Aging of the OMAS GEGEN RECHTS
item.dc:creator: Ricarda Drüeke, Tanja von Braunmühl
item.description:
Media and Communication · Ricarda Drüeke, Tanja von Braunmühl

Topics: Visual activism, Social media activism, Instagram, Digital activism

The article analyzes the visual activism of OMAS GEGEN RECHTS (“Grannies against the right”), a movement founded in Austria in 2017 by older feminist women mobilizing against far-right politics. The movement increasingly extends into digital spaces, where political conflict over democratic values and public legitimacy is negotiated. At the same time, forms of protest by older activists remain largely unexplored. Drawing on concepts of agonistic publics, visual activism, and unruliness, we analyze how OMAS GEGEN RECHTS engage with digital media to articulate political positions and intervene in right-wing politics. The study is based on a qualitative analysis of visual practices in Instagram posts published in 2025, focusing on the nationwide account representing Austria: @omasgegenrechts (137K followers in late December 2025). We examine how visual practices are used to mobilize supporters, construct collective identities, and contest right-wing narratives. Our findings reveal how images and symbolic self-representation are used to counter ageist exclusions from digital spaces while simultaneously mobilizing both members of the movement and broader publics. Rather than being marginalized by digital divides, OMAS GEGEN RECHTS actively negotiate platform constraints and transform age into a source of political legitimacy and moral authority. By emphasizing age and visibility as central dimensions of digital conflict, this article contributes to debates on digital media, activism, and political struggles.

item.title: Digital Fem-Washing of War: Olena Zelenska’s Vogue Cover and the #sitlikeagirl Campaign
item.dc:creator: Karolina Szpyrko
item.description:
Media and Communication · Karolina Szpyrko

Topics: Social media activism, Political communication, Misinformation, Digital activism

This article examines the media controversy surrounding Olena Zelenska’s 2022 Vogue photoshoot, including audience reactions, subsequent news coverage, and the feminist social media campaign #sitlikeagirl. It investigates how feminist discourse became mobilised within highly mediatised wartime communication. Drawing on conjunctural cross-platform analysis of social media posts, Instagram comments, and news coverage, the study reveals a significant discrepancy between dominant journalistic framings of the controversy and the discourse visible within the original comment sections. While media coverage repeatedly framed Zelenska as targeted by misogynistic criticism concerning her allegedly “unfeminine” posture, the analysed comments predominantly criticised the political and aesthetic implications of glamourising war through fashion media. The article argues that the viral feminist framing of the campaign emerged less as a direct response to observable sexism and more as a participatory and affective form of wartime digital communication shaped by platform logics, emotional alignment, and recognisable postfeminist activist aesthetics. Situating the campaign within broader debates on participatory war, misinformation, digital activism, and nation branding, the article proposes the concept of digital fem-washing of war to describe how feminist visibility and activist language become incorporated into the communicative infrastructures of contemporary hypermediated warfare.

item.title: Cyber-Militia and Digital Coercion: Online Targeting and Militarised Communication in Burkina Faso
item.dc:creator: Samba Dialimpa Badji, Harouna Drabo
item.description:
Media and Communication · Samba Dialimpa Badji, Harouna Drabo

Topics: Digital media, Political communication, Propaganda, Online harassment

This article examines the emergence of coordinated pro-regime digital networks in Burkina Faso through the concept of “cyber-militia.” Drawing on a comparative qualitative analysis of 468 Facebook entries collected across three online targeting campaigns, the study explores how actors associated with the Brigade d’intervention rapide de la communication (BIR-C) use digital platforms to amplify hostile narratives, intimidate critics, and delegitimise individuals and organisations perceived as threats to the military regime. Combining qualitative content analysis and process tracing, the article identifies three operational logics of cyber-militia communication: escalation and intimidation, persistence and reputational delegitimisation, and institutional delegitimisation. The findings suggest that cyber-militias function as hybrid formations situated at the intersection of propaganda, participatory digital culture, and coercive state power. The article contributes to scholarship on digital media and conflict by proposing cyber-militia as a new analytical framework for understanding coordinated forms of participatory digital coercion in contemporary conflict environments.

item.title: The science of beauty: Looksmaxxing, self-help, and genetic fatalism in women’s online spaces
item.dc:creator: Rachel Bergmann, Elizabeth Fetterolf
item.description:
New Media & Society · Rachel Bergmann, Elizabeth Fetterolf

Topics: Gender representation, Social media discourse, Digital communication, Visual communication

This paper examines the emergence of “looksmaxxing” in women’s online spaces. As a specific and underexamined element within what Jilly Boyce Kay analyzes as “reactionary feminism,” essentialist logics about gender and race are operationalized through the aesthetics of science and self-optimization rather than explicitly political rhetoric. Users construct the “science of beauty” through decentralized forms of expertise, from plastic surgery influencers to scientific racism to community-generated aesthetic taxonomies. We identify a thread of individualized and intimate genetic fatalism shaping both aesthetic frameworks and the tactics used to achieve them, mutating the postfeminist promise of self-transformation toward distinctly reactionary goals. This tension between the essentialism and malleability of the body makes the paradigm generative and self-sustaining, absorbing failure and keeping users invested. This case is a call to examine “fringe” and aesthetics-focused cultural formations for insight on how bioessentialist ideas about race and gender circulate today.

item.title: Transnational news repertoires are associated with patterns of emotional responses to war: A case study of Russian speakers in Germany
item.dc:creator: Eunike Piwoni, Anna Ryzhova, Florian Toepfl
item.description:
Journalism · Eunike Piwoni, Anna Ryzhova, Florian Toepfl

Topics: Media use, News consumption, Media effects, Emotion regulation

Research on distant suffering has documented diverse emotional responses to violent conflict. Yet few studies have set out to examine how audiences’ emotional responses may be associated with their news repertoires. Addressing this gap, this study asks whether and how migrant audiences’ transnational news repertoires are associated with their emotional responses to a war to which they are connected through one of the conflict parties. Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews with Russian-speaking migrants in Germany, the study examines their emotional responses to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine since February 2022. The findings identify four news repertoire types, each closely associated with a distinct emotional response pattern. Especially stark differences emerge between democratic and pro-Kremlin repertoire users. While the former expressed predominantly negative emotions and sometimes considered personal guilt, the latter reported relief at Russia’s attack, a sense of being discriminated against in Germany, and renewed pride in Russia. The study advances the literature on distant suffering by identifying news repertoires as an important factor associated with specific emotional response patterns and by showing that witnessing suffering from a distance may elicit not only negative but also positive emotions.

item.title: Artificial intelligence and journalism in Ibero-America: A comparative study of perceptions, practices and challenges
item.dc:creator: Paulo Nuno Vicente, Sara Pérez‐Seijo, Suzana Barbosa
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Paulo Nuno Vicente, Sara Pérez‐Seijo, Suzana Barbosa

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Journalistic practice, Professional norms, Digital transformation

This article explores the perceptions, practices, challenges and opportunities associated with the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in journalistic practice within the Ibero-American context. Drawing on an original quantitative comparative study conducted in Portugal, Spain and Brazil, the research investigates how professional journalists understand, engage with and respond to the integration of AI-driven tools in newsrooms. Based on survey data from 271 journalists, the findings reveal widespread but predominantly basic knowledge of AI, general curiosity and cautious optimism regarding its implementation, and notable concern about its impact on professional ethics, job security, and editorial transparency. The study highlights significant variations across countries in the use of AI applications. Key challenges identified include the absence of formal editorial guidelines, limited training opportunities and a lack of transparency in the use of AI-generated content. The research underscores the urgent need for institutional strategies that ensure responsible AI integration, safeguard journalistic standards and support professional development.

item.title: AI for Democracy? How Public Service Media Around the World Use Artificial Intelligence to Produce Journalism
item.dc:creator: Kate Wright, Melissa Terras
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Kate Wright, Melissa Terras

Topics: Public service media, Artificial intelligence in journalism, Journalistic practice, Democratic discourse

We examine how public service media (PSM) around the world use AI to assist journalism production. Using surveys, organizational documents, and interviews with senior managers from PSMs in Africa, Asia, Europe, Oceania, and the Caribbean, we map which AI tools PSMs use, how they use them, and how they navigate the relationship between efficiency, PSM values, and their broader democratic purpose. We analyze participating PSMs’ use of AI in transcription, image generation/editing, and content customization for online and social media. Other uses, including translation, synthetic voices, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation, AI “presenters,” and facial recognition, are also discussed. We argue that participants’ uses of AI, and the tools they deploy, are not particularly distinctive: a key driver is also time and cost savings. However, we argue that the use of AI by these PSMs does involve uniquely complex challenges relating to marked tensions between efficiency objectives and PSM values, between PSM values themselves, and between PSMs’ efforts to fulfil their statutory obligations to audiences and their broader democratic mission. This study provides the first broadly-based international study on PSMs’ use of AI, highlighting the difficulties they face in safeguarding democratic journalistic values despite rising costs and budget cuts.

item.title: Configuring Journalistic Users: How Software Design Shapes News Work
item.dc:creator: Torbjörn Rolandsson
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Torbjörn Rolandsson

Topics: Journalistic practice, Newsroom practices, Digital journalism, Human-computer interaction

Drawing on an ethnography of Astrid, the Swedish public-service broadcaster SVT's Content Management System, this paper contributes theoretical and empirical insights to studies of design in journalism. The paper develops a four-mechanism heuristic for studying how software development configures journalistic users and workflows. The four mechanisms – organizational configuration, user knowledge production, stabilization, and negotiation – provide a structured way of examining how design work is organized, how journalistic users are made knowable, how preferred forms of journalistic work become inscribed into technical systems, and how those inscriptions are negotiated in practice. Applying the heuristic to Astrid demonstrates how designers and product owners in news organizations can be active participants in producing normative visions about journalism and inscribing them in technologies, thereby shaping aspects of journalistic work.

item.title: One Country, Two Approaches: How Belgium’s PSM Engages Young People with News
item.dc:creator: Juanma Prieto-Arosa, José Moriano, José Miguel Túñez-López
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Juanma Prieto-Arosa, José Moriano, José Miguel Túñez-López

Topics: Public service media, Journalism, Social media platforms, News consumption

This study compares two Belgian digital-first Public Service Media (PSM) initiatives targeting teenagers: RTBF’s Mise à Jour and VRT’s nws.nws.nws.. Using institutional documents and 13 semi-structured interviews, it analyses editorial strategy, participation, production, distribution and impact assessment. Both use platform-native formats and explanatory journalism, rejecting infantilisation. Mise à Jour follows an editorial and cultural translation model, adapting selected topics to TikTok and Instagram, whereas nws.nws.nws. adopts a relational model in which user questions shape editorial relevance. Participation remains consultative, while platform dependence generates tensions over algorithmic visibility, representation, editorial autonomy and sustainability. These findings extend the platform paradox into a public service paradox: commercial platforms enable PSM to reach teenagers while pressuring universality, inclusivity and independent definitions of public value. Sustainable renewal therefore requires stable resources, more inclusive representation and evaluation beyond engagement metrics.

item.title: Mapping Cognitive Geographies of Journalism: Professional Imaginaries Across the Local-National Divide in Portugal
item.dc:creator: Rui Alexandre Novais, Filipe Resende, Ângela Maria Teixeira Leite
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Rui Alexandre Novais, Filipe Resende, Ângela Maria Teixeira Leite

Topics: Journalism studies, Journalistic roles, Professional identity, Digital journalism

This study maps the cognitive geography of Portuguese journalism, exploring how the local-national divide shapes professional imaginaries across platforms, formats, and news cultures. Drawing on Media Geography, Network Society Theory, Deep Mediatization, and Cultural Industries, we conceptualize journalistic self-perceptions as a dynamic system structured by spatial hierarchies, technological infrastructures, and industrial segmentation. Using data from the 2023 Portuguese Worlds of Journalism Study, we employ descriptive analysis, cross-tabulation, and t-tests to map the relational interplay of scale and technology. We find marked asymmetries between local and national actors, showing how technological embeddedness and industrial segmentation crystallize into distinct professional habitus. The study advances mapping as a critical method for diagnosing symbolic boundaries and structural inequalities in journalism's cognitive geography.

item.title: The Political Leaning of Fact-Checking: Countering Italian Disinformation on the War in Ukraine
item.dc:creator: Tommaso Valastro, Sergio Splendore
item.description:
Media and Communication · Tommaso Valastro, Sergio Splendore

Topics: Fact-checking, Misinformation, Political polarization, Selective exposure

The intense disinformation efforts that accompanied Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine highlight the importance of countering misinformation to mitigate the influence of foreign actors, particularly in vulnerable public spheres such as the Italian one. Despite widespread use, the effectiveness of fact-checking in correcting misinformation remains ambiguous, with limited exploration of the underlying reasons. This article focuses on the role of political leaning and partisanship in shaping individuals’ comprehension of factual information, their inclination to fact-checking exposure, and their capacity to assimilate findings that challenge their preconceived beliefs. We measure the role of these variables for 10 different statements about Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, employing original survey data collected in Italy in spring 2022. We find veracity assessment to be associated with partisan views of the war for both true and false statements, with Russia-leaning views frequently correlating with lower exposure to and reception of fact-checks. Right-leaning political attitudes often work in the same direction, in some cases amplifying the partisan rejection of fact-checks. These findings contribute to literature on fact-checking, selective exposure, motivated reasoning, and misinformation, corroborating previous studies on the limits of debunking efforts and extending their insights to a setting well known for its high level of political parallelism. A crucial implication of these results is that political attitudes should receive greater consideration when addressing misinformation and foreign disinformation efforts, given their potential to amplify partisan barriers that moderate the corrective power of fact-checking. Furthermore, this partisan acceptance of fact-checks complicates the normative assessment of journalistic practices.

item.title: TikTok as a Site for Ethno-Political Contestations and Conflict Mediation Among Ethiopian Diaspora
item.dc:creator: Abdissa Zerai, Gizachew Nemomsa
item.description:
Media and Communication · Abdissa Zerai, Gizachew Nemomsa

Topics: TikTok, Social media discourse, Political polarization, Digital diaspora

This study examines how TikTok has served as a site for both ethno-political contestations and conflict mediation in the context of Ethiopia by focusing on the engagement of the Ethiopian diasporic community on the platform. Informed by the deliberative democratic theoretical framework, it addresses how ethno-political contestations among the diasporic community discursively manifest themselves in the TikTok sphere and how such diasporic community mediates the contestations on the platform. In addressing these, critical discourse analysis was employed on purposively selected TikTok content created from October 2023 to September 2024 across four key thematic areas. The findings indicate that the ethno-political contestations among the diasporic community manifested themselves on the TikTok sphere by juxtaposing exclusionary ethnic identity against inclusive pan-Ethiopian identity. Such contestations were enacted through the deployment of charged rhetoric. However, the contestations were mediated by pushing back against destructive discursive trends through strategic intervention of some TikTok hosts. The platform served as a site for both an ideological battlefield and a counter-platform for challenging polemical discourses and for promoting deliberative discourse among the Ethiopian diaspora. Contrary to the prevailing skepticism about TikTok’s potential for meaningful discourse, this study reveals that if deployed strategically, it can be a valuable platform for advancing rational dialogue among disparate groups, which could be instrumental in encouraging participants to seek collective solutions for enduring political problems.

item.title: Foreign Faces in the False: Immigrant-Targeting False Posts on Social Media and Their Impact on Immigrant Perceptions
item.dc:creator: Mingxiao Sui, Ian Hawkins
item.description:
Communication Research · Mingxiao Sui, Ian Hawkins

Topics: Misinformation, Fact-checking, Social media, Immigrant perceptions

This work investigates three interrelated questions around false information targeting immigrants as a broad social group on U.S. social media (thereafter referred to as immigrant-targeting false SNS claims). Study 1 examines content-level features that potentially attract readers’ attention: a quantitative analysis of PolitiFact data showed that relative to those not specifically about immigrants, immigrant-targeting false SNS claims exhibited a stronger negative tone and were more about race-related issues. Study 2 experimentally investigates the effects of immigrant-targeting SNS claims with distinctive media frames (defined as claims emphasizing either economic or health-related concerns) and that of corrective approach (with vs. without fact-checking flags): participants who viewed immigrant-targeting SNS claims flagged as false reported lower threat and anxiety perceptions and higher positive trait perceptions than those who viewed unflagged claims. Regarding the reference groups—specifically, “legal” versus “illegal” immigrants—participants associated with their perceived anxiety, the effect of fact-checking flags was conditional on the SNS claims’ media frames. Study 2 also uncovered that cognitive reflection and actively open-minded thinking play distinct roles in shaping how people respond to immigrant-targeting misinformation and fact-checking labels.

item.title: Symptom-Level Comorbidity Patterns Between Depression and Internet Gaming Disorder Among Adolescents: Evidence from Longitudinal Network Analysis with Gender Considerations
item.dc:creator: Shiyun Chen, Yue Zhao, Xinli Chi, Shimin Zhu
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Shiyun Chen, Yue Zhao, Xinli Chi, Shimin Zhu

Topics: Mental health, Adolescent mental health, Video games, Longitudinal study

Adolescence is a period with an increased risk for the co-occurrence of depression and Internet gaming disorder (IGD), yet we still know little about how specific symptoms of these two conditions influence each other over time. In this study, we applied cross-lagged panel network analysis to two-wave data from a community sample of 538 adolescents (Mean age = 12.51 years; 53.7 percent female). Potential gender differences in the network structure were examined. In the overall sample and in both gender groups, depressive symptoms consistently predicted later gaming-related problems, whereas no reverse cross-disorder pathways were retained. In particular, suicidal ideation and psychomotor symptoms emerged as bridge symptoms linking depression and IGD, while sleep problems showed moderate outgoing expected influence in the overall symptom network. While boys and girls showed broadly similar patterns, some differences emerged in how specific symptoms were connected and which symptoms were most influential. These findings clarify the longitudinal symptom-level associations between depression and IGD in adolescents, suggesting that addressing key depressive symptoms may help reduce the risk of later IGD.

item.title: Cognitive Surrender: When Artificial Intelligence Does Our Thinking for Us
item.dc:creator: Brenda K. Wiederhold
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Brenda K. Wiederhold

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Human-AI interaction, Cognitive processing, Generative AI

item.title: Beyond quality control: Peer-feedback and team culture in virtual journalistic teams
item.dc:creator: Minna Koivula, Kaisa Lindholm
item.description:
Journalism · Minna Koivula, Kaisa Lindholm

Topics: Journalistic practice, Newsroom practices, Computer-mediated communication, Organizational communication

Previous research has approached feedback in journalism from an operational view, that is, as a quality control process between the journalist and the editor. Challenging this view, this study examines peer-feedback, that is, feedback between the members of a journalistic team, and asks what are its characteristics, meanings, and functions in technology-mediated teamwork. We define feedback as a team level communicative process, with constitutive power and relational qualities in addition to task-related purposes. Our mixed methods analysis centers on the Slack messages of a team of journalists, and shows that peer-feedback is constitutive of team culture. Our findings broaden journalism studies’ view of feedback beyond its role as a quality control mechanism, shed light on how peer-feedback materializes in newsroom collaboration and offer a conceptual tool for future feedback-related research.

item.title: How media organisations and non-governmental organisations support or practice journalism in conflict settings
item.dc:creator: Martina Hrgovic, Sonja Kretzschmar, Judith Pies, Annika Sehl, Christoph Neuberger, Verena Wassink, Linda Henke
item.description:
Journalism · Martina Hrgovic, Sonja Kretzschmar, Judith Pies, Annika Sehl, Christoph Neuberger, Verena Wassink, Linda Henke

Topics: Journalism, Conflict journalism, Peacebuilding, Non-governmental organizations

Journalism in conflict settings increasingly involves actors beyond traditional media organisations. While non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and media organisations (MOs) have distinct identities, both operate in overlapping spaces of information production, dialogue facilitation and peacebuilding support. Yet, their interaction remains underexplored.
